title: No. 70 — The Executive Department Further Considered (Hamilton)
paragraphs: There is an idea, not without its advocates, that a vigorous Executive is inconsistent with the character of republican government. The enlightened friends of this kind of government must at least hope that the supposition has no foundation, since they could never admit it to be true without also condemning their own principles. Energy in the Executive is a leading feature in the definition of good government. It is essential to protecting the community against foreign attacks. It is no less essential to the steady administration of the laws, and to protecting property against those irregular and high-handed combinations that sometimes interrupt the ordinary course of justice. It is essential as well to securing liberty against the enterprises and assaults of ambition, of faction and of anarchy. Anyone with the slightest knowledge of Roman history knows how often that republic had to take refuge in the absolute power of a single man, under the formidable title of Dictator. It did so against the intrigues of ambitious individuals who aspired to tyranny, and against the seditions of whole classes of the community whose conduct threatened the existence of all government, as well as against the invasions of foreign enemies who threatened to conquer and destroy Rome.

There is no need, however, to pile up more arguments or examples on this point. A feeble Executive means a feeble execution of the government. A feeble execution is only another way of saying a bad execution. And a government that is badly executed, whatever it may be in theory, must be a bad government in practice.

Taking it for granted, then, that all sensible men will agree on the necessity of an energetic Executive, it remains only to ask what ingredients make up this energy. How far can they be combined with the other ingredients that make up safety in the republican sense? And how far does that combination mark the plan reported by the Convention?
The ingredients that make up energy in the Executive are, first, unity; second, duration; third, an adequate provision for its support; fourth, competent powers.
The ingredients that make up safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people; second, a due responsibility.

The politicians and statesmen most celebrated for the soundness of their principles and the justice of their views have declared in favor of a single Executive and a numerous legislature. They have rightly regarded energy as the most necessary quality of the former, and have held that it is best found in power placed in a single hand. With equal justice they have regarded the latter as best suited to deliberation and wisdom, and best fitted to win the confidence of the people and secure their rights and interests.

No one will dispute that unity promotes energy. Decision, activity, secrecy and dispatch will generally mark the proceedings of one man far more strongly than those of any larger number, and as the number grows, these qualities will diminish.

This unity may be destroyed in two ways. One is by vesting the power in two or more chief executives of equal dignity and authority. The other is by vesting it ostensibly in one man who is subject, wholly or in part, to the control and cooperation of others serving as his counselors. The two Consuls of Rome may serve as an example of the first. Examples of the second we shall find in the constitutions of several of the States. New York and New Jersey, if I remember rightly, are the only States that have entrusted the executive authority wholly to single men.(1) Both these ways of destroying the unity of the Executive have their partisans, but the supporters of an executive council are the more numerous. Both are open to similar objections, if not equal ones, and may in most respects be examined together.

The experience of other nations will teach us little on this subject. Insofar as it teaches anything, however, it teaches us not to be fond of plurality in the Executive. We have seen that the Achaeans, after trying two Praetors, were led to abolish one. Roman history records many instances of harm to the republic from quarrels between the Consuls, and between the military Tribunes who were at times substituted for the Consuls. But it gives us no example of any particular advantage the state gained from having several of these officials. That their quarrels were not more frequent or more fatal is a matter of astonishment, until we notice the unusual position in which the republic was almost continually placed, and the prudent policy that circumstances pointed out and the Consuls followed, of dividing the government between them. The patricians were engaged in a perpetual struggle with the plebeians to preserve their ancient authorities and dignities. The Consuls, who were generally chosen from the former body, were commonly united by their personal interest in defending the privileges of their order. Beyond this motive for unity, after the arms of the republic had greatly widened the bounds of its empire, it became the established custom for the Consuls to divide the administration between themselves by lot. One of them stayed at Rome to govern the city and its surroundings, and the other took command in the more distant provinces. This expedient must, no doubt, have done much to prevent the collisions and rivalries that might otherwise have disturbed the peace of the republic.

But if we leave the dim light of historical research and rely purely on the dictates of reason and good sense, we shall find much greater cause to reject than to approve the idea of plurality in the Executive, in any form whatever.

Wherever two or more persons are engaged in a common undertaking or pursuit, there is always a danger of differences of opinion. If it is a public trust or office, in which they are clothed with equal dignity and authority, there is a special danger of personal rivalry and even hostility. From either of these causes, and especially from all of them together, the bitterest quarrels are likely to spring. Whenever they occur, they lower the respect given to those they divide, weaken their authority, and distract their plans and actions. If they should unfortunately strike the supreme executive office of a country that consists of several persons, they might block or defeat the most important measures of the government in the most critical emergencies of the state. And what is still worse, they might split the community into the most violent and irreconcilable factions, attached in different ways to the different individuals who made up the executive.

Men often oppose a thing merely because they had no hand in planning it, or because it was planned by people they dislike. But if they were consulted and happened to disapprove, opposition then becomes, in their eyes, an indispensable duty of self-love. They seem to think themselves bound in honor, and by every motive of personal infallibility, to defeat whatever has been resolved contrary to their views. Men of upright and benevolent temperament have too many occasions to observe, with horror, to what desperate lengths this disposition is sometimes carried, and how often the great interests of society are sacrificed to the vanity, the conceit and the obstinacy of individuals who have enough credit to make their passions and whims matter to the public. Perhaps the question now before the public may in its consequences furnish melancholy proofs of the effects of this contemptible weakness, or rather detestable vice, in human character.

On the principles of a free government, drawbacks from the source just mentioned must necessarily be accepted in forming the legislature. But it is unnecessary, and therefore unwise, to introduce them into the constitution of the Executive. It is here, too, that they may do the most harm. In the legislature, quickness of decision is oftener an evil than a benefit. The differences of opinion and the wrangling of parties in that department, though they may sometimes obstruct beneficial plans, often promote deliberation and caution and help to check excesses by the majority. Moreover, once a resolution has been taken, the opposition must end. That resolution is a law, and resistance to it is punishable. But no favorable circumstance softens or makes up for the disadvantages of dissension in the executive department. Here they are pure and unmixed. There is no point at which they cease to operate. They embarrass and weaken the carrying out of the plan or measure they relate to, from the first step to the last. They constantly work against those qualities of the Executive that are the most necessary ingredients in its composition, vigor and expedition, and this without any compensating good. In the conduct of war, in which the energy of the Executive is the bulwark of national security, everything would be to be feared from its plurality.

It must be confessed that these observations apply with the greatest weight to the first case supposed, that is, to a plurality of chief executives of equal dignity and authority, a scheme whose advocates are not likely to form a numerous sect. But they apply, though not with equal weight, still with considerable weight, to the project of a council whose concurrence is made constitutionally necessary to the operations of the ostensible Executive. A scheming cabal in that council would be able to distract and enervate the whole system of administration. If no such cabal should exist, the mere diversity of views and opinions would be enough to tinge the exercise of executive authority with a spirit of habitual feebleness and delay.

(Yet among the weightiest objections to a plurality in the Executive, an objection that holds as much against the council plan as against the first, is that it tends to hide faults and destroy responsibility. Responsibility is of two kinds, to censure and to punishment. The first is the more important of the two, especially in an elective office. A man in public trust will much more often act in a way that makes him unworthy of being trusted any longer than in a way that makes him liable to legal punishment. But multiplying the Executive makes detection harder in either case. Amid mutual accusations it often becomes impossible to decide on whom the blame or the punishment for a harmful measure, or series of harmful measures, should really fall. It is shifted from one to another with so much skill, and under such plausible appearances, that public opinion is left in suspense about the real author. The circumstances that may have led to a national failure or misfortune are sometimes so complicated that, where a number of actors may have had different degrees and kinds of involvement, we may clearly see on the whole that there has been mismanagement and yet find it impossible to say to whose account the resulting evil is truly chargeable.)(E1)

"I was overruled by my council. The council were so divided in their opinions that it was impossible to obtain any better resolution on the point." These and similar excuses are constantly at hand, whether true or false. And who will take the trouble, or bear the ill will, of a strict inquiry into the secret springs of the transaction? Suppose a citizen is found zealous enough to undertake the unpromising task. If the parties concerned happen to be in collusion, it is easy for them to wrap the circumstances in so much ambiguity that no one can tell what any of them precisely did.

In the one case where the governor of this State is joined with a council, that is, in appointing to offices, we have seen the harms of it from the point of view now under consideration. Scandalous appointments to important offices have been made. Some cases, indeed, have been so flagrant that ALL PARTIES have agreed the thing was improper. When inquiry has been made, the governor has put the blame on the members of the council, who in turn have charged it to his nomination, while the people remain altogether at a loss to say whose influence put their interests into hands so unqualified and so obviously improper. Out of tenderness to individuals, I refrain from going into particulars.

It is evident from these considerations that a plurality in the Executive tends to deprive the people of the two greatest securities they can have for the faithful exercise of any delegated power. The first is the restraint of public opinion, which loses its effectiveness, both because the censure that attends bad measures is divided among a number of people and because it is uncertain on whom it ought to fall. The second is the opportunity to discover easily and clearly the misconduct of the persons they trust, so as either to remove them from office or, in cases that allow it, to punish them.

In England the king is a perpetual chief executive, and for the sake of public peace it has become an accepted maxim that he is not accountable for his administration and that his person is sacred. Nothing, therefore, can be wiser in that kingdom than to attach to the king a constitutional council, who may be responsible to the nation for the advice they give. Without this there would be no responsibility whatever in the executive department, an idea not to be admitted in a free government. But even there the king is not bound by the resolutions of his council, though they are answerable for the advice they give. He is the absolute master of his own conduct in the exercise of his office, and may follow or disregard the counsel given him at his sole discretion.

But in a republic, where every public official ought to be personally responsible for his conduct in office, the reason that in the British Constitution makes a council proper not only ceases to apply but turns against the institution. In the monarchy of Great Britain, the council serves as a substitute for the forbidden responsibility of the chief executive, and to some degree as a hostage to national justice for his good behavior. In the American republic, it would serve to destroy, or greatly reduce, the intended and necessary responsibility of the chief executive himself.

The idea of a council to the Executive, which has so generally been adopted in the State constitutions, was drawn from that maxim of republican jealousy which holds power to be safer in the hands of a number of men than of a single man. Even if the maxim were admitted to apply to this case, I would maintain that the advantage on that side would not outweigh the many disadvantages on the other. But I do not think the rule applies to the executive power at all. In this I clearly agree with a writer whom the celebrated Junius pronounces to be "deep, solid, and ingenious," who holds that "the executive power is more easily confined when it is ONE";(2) that it is far safer for the people's jealousy and watchfulness to have a single object; and, in a word, that every multiplication of the Executive is more dangerous than friendly to liberty.

A little consideration will satisfy us that the kind of security sought through multiplying the Executive cannot be had. The numbers must be so large as to make combination difficult, or else they are a source of danger rather than security. The united credit and influence of several individuals must be more formidable to liberty than the credit and influence of any one of them alone. When power is placed in the hands of so small a number of men that their interests and views can easily be combined in a common enterprise by a skillful leader, it becomes more liable to abuse, and more dangerous when abused, than if it were lodged in one man. Such a man, by the very fact of being alone, will be more closely watched and more readily suspected, and cannot gather so great a mass of influence as when he is associated with others. The Decemvirs of Rome, whose name denotes their number,(3) were more to be dreaded in their usurpation than any ONE of them would have been. No one would think of proposing an Executive much more numerous than that body; from six to a dozen have been suggested as the size of the council. Even the largest of these numbers is not too large for an easy combination, and from such a combination America would have more to fear than from the ambition of any single individual. A council to a chief executive who is himself responsible for what he does is generally nothing better than a clog on his good intentions, is often the instrument and accomplice of his bad ones, and is almost always a cloak for his faults.

I refrain from dwelling on the subject of expense. Yet it is evident that if the council were numerous enough to serve the principal end the institution aims at, the salaries of its members, who would have to be drawn from their homes to live at the seat of government, would make an item among the public expenditures too serious to be incurred for an object of doubtful usefulness. I will only add that before the Constitution appeared, I seldom met an intelligent man from any of the States who did not admit, as a result of experience, that the UNITY of the executive of this State was one of the best distinguishing features of our constitution.

1. New York has no council except for the single purpose of appointing to offices; New Jersey has a council whom the governor may consult. But I think, from the terms of the constitution, their resolutions do not bind him.
